name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q01 - Basic tissue types in complex animals

questiontext.text: How many basic types of tissues are present in all complex animals, and which organ is explicitly stated to contain all of them?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In multicellular animals, a group of similar cells along with intercellular substances performs a specific function and is organised into a tissue.

Step 2: Evaluation of Tissue Classification
All complex animals consist of only four basic types of tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, and neural.

Step 3: Application to Organ Organisation
These four basic tissues are organised in specific proportions and patterns to form organs; the human heart is a classic example consisting of all four tissue types.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Complex animals consist of four basic types of tissues, and the heart contains all four types.

answer.text: Four basic types; heart
Three basic types; stomach
Five basic types; kidney
Six basic types; lung

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q02 - Function and location of squamous epithelium

questiontext.text: Which type of simple epithelium is made of a single thin layer of flattened cells with irregular boundaries and is involved in forming a diffusion boundary?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Simple epithelium is composed of a single layer of cells and is subdivided based on cell shape into squamous, cuboidal, and columnar types.

Step 2: Evaluation of Squamous Epithelium
Squamous epithelium consists of a single thin layer of flattened cells with irregular boundaries, found in the walls of blood vessels and air sacs of lungs where it forms a diffusion boundary.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The tissue described is simple squamous epithelium.

answer.text: Cuboidal epithelium
Squamous epithelium
Columnar epithelium
Compound epithelium

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q03 - Epithelium of proximal convoluted tubule

questiontext.text: The epithelium lining the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of a nephron in the kidney is characterised by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cuboidal epithelium is composed of a single layer of cube-like cells commonly found in ducts of glands and tubular parts of nephrons, performing secretion and absorption.

Step 2: Application to PCT
To increase the surface area for reabsorption in the kidney, the cuboidal epithelium of the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) bears microvilli on its free surface.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The PCT of a nephron is lined by cuboidal epithelium with microvilli.

answer.text: Flattened squamous cells with cilia
Multi-layered compound epithelium
Cuboidal epithelium with microvilli
Tall columnar cells with cilia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q04 - Nuclear position in columnar epithelium

questiontext.text: Where are the nuclei located in the tall and slender cells of simple columnar epithelium lining the stomach and intestine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Simple columnar epithelium is composed of a single layer of tall and slender cells specialised for secretion and absorption.

Step 2: Structural Evaluation
In simple columnar epithelial cells, the nuclei are characteristically located at the base of the cells, while the free apical surface may possess microvilli.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The nuclei of simple columnar epithelial cells are located at the base.

answer.text: At the apical free surface
Strictly in the central region
Absent in mature cells
At the base of the cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q05 - Exocrine vs endocrine gland secretions

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of secretions is released exclusively through ducts or tubes by exocrine glands?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Based on the mode of pouring of their secretions, glands are divided into exocrine glands (with ducts) and endocrine glands (ductless).

Step 2: Evaluation of Secretions
Exocrine glands secrete mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk, digestive enzymes, and other cell products through ducts or tubes. Endocrine glands lack ducts and secrete hormones directly into the fluid bathing the gland.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk, and digestive enzymes are all exocrine secretions.

answer.text: Mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk, and digestive enzymes
Hormones, saliva, earwax, and digestive enzymes
Mucus, hormones, milk, and oil
Hormones and digestive enzymes only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q06 - Locations of compound epithelium

questiontext.text: Compound epithelium is found covering all of the following surfaces EXCEPT:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Compound epithelium is multi-layered and primarily provides protection against chemical and mechanical stresses.

Step 2: Evaluation of Locations
Compound epithelium covers the dry surface of the skin, the moist surface of the buccal cavity, pharynx, and the inner lining of ducts of salivary glands and pancreatic ducts. In contrast, the air sacs of lungs require a thin diffusion boundary and are lined by simple squamous epithelium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Compound epithelium does not line the air sacs of the lungs.

answer.text: Moist surface of the buccal cavity
Air sacs of the lungs
Inner lining of ducts of salivary glands
Inner lining of pancreatic ducts

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q07 - Function of tight junctions in epithelium

questiontext.text: Which specialised cell junction prevents substances from leaking across an epithelial tissue?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Three types of cell junctions provide structural and functional links between individual cells in epithelium and other tissues: tight, adhering, and gap junctions.

Step 2: Functional Comparison
Tight junctions seal intercellular spaces to stop substances from leaking across a tissue. Adhering junctions perform cementing to keep neighbouring cells together, and gap junctions connect cytoplasm for rapid transfer of ions and small molecules.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Tight junctions prevent substances from leaking across a tissue.

answer.text: Gap junctions
Adhering junctions
Tight junctions
Intercalated discs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q08 - Origin and types of glandular epithelium

questiontext.text: Glandular epithelium is formed by the specialisation of which cell types, and which pair correctly represents unicellular and multicellular glands respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Some epithelial cells become specialised for secretion and constitute glandular epithelium.

Step 2: Evaluation of Cell Origin and Examples
Specifically, some of the columnar or cuboidal cells get specialised for secretion. Unicellular glands consist of isolated glandular cells, such as goblet cells of the alimentary canal, whereas multicellular glands consist of clusters of cells, such as the salivary gland.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Glandular epithelium arises from columnar or cuboidal cells, with goblet cells as unicellular glands and salivary glands as multicellular glands.

answer.text: Squamous or cuboidal cells; salivary gland and goblet cells
Squamous or columnar cells; goblet cells and salivary gland
Compound epithelial cells; pancreatic duct and goblet cells
Columnar or cuboidal cells; goblet cells and salivary gland

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q09 - Ciliated epithelium vs microvilli functions

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately distinguishes ciliated epithelium from microvilli-bearing epithelium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Free surfaces of simple epithelial cells may bear cilia or microvilli, each serving a distinct physiological role.

Step 2: Evaluation of Functional Differences
Ciliated epithelium (columnar or cuboidal cells bearing cilia) moves particles or mucus in a specific direction over the epithelium in hollow organs like bronchioles and fallopian tubes. In contrast, microvilli (seen in the PCT of nephrons and the intestine) increase surface area for absorption and secretion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ciliated epithelium moves particles or mucus in a specific direction in bronchioles and fallopian tubes, whereas microvilli-bearing epithelium is present in the PCT and intestine for secretion and absorption.

answer.text: Ciliated epithelium moves particles or mucus in a specific direction in bronchioles and fallopian tubes, whereas microvilli occur in PCT and intestine to aid secretion and absorption
Ciliated epithelium occurs only in squamous cells of blood vessels, whereas microvilli occur exclusively in the skin
Both cilia and microvilli are restricted to compound epithelium to prevent mechanical stress
Ciliated epithelium is non-motile and forms a diffusion boundary, whereas microvilli propel ova through fallopian tubes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q10 - Morphology vs anatomy and evolutionary trend

questiontext.text: In animal biology, how does the conventional meaning of "anatomy" differ from "morphology", and what does the study of organs across evolutionary levels reveal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Morphology and anatomy are distinct terms used when studying the organisation of multicellular organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation of Definitions
In animals, morphology refers to the external appearance of the organs or parts of the body, whereas anatomy conventionally refers to the study of the morphology of internal organs. Furthermore, complexity in organs and organ systems displays a discernible evolutionary trend.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Morphology studies external appearance, anatomy studies internal organs, and their complexity shows an evolutionary trend.

answer.text: Morphology studies internal organs, anatomy studies external features, and organs show no evolutionary trend
Morphology refers to external appearance, anatomy refers to internal organs, and organ complexity displays an evolutionary trend
Both morphology and anatomy refer exclusively to cellular junctions in invertebrates
Anatomy is used only for plants and microbes, while morphology is used only for vertebrates

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q11 - Matrix composition of connective tissue

questiontext.text: In connective tissues (except blood), the matrix or ground substance accumulating between cells and fibres is primarily composed of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Connective tissues consist of cells, protein fibres (collagen or elastin), and an extracellular ground substance (matrix).

Step 2: Evaluation of Matrix Composition
Connective tissue cells secrete modified polysaccharides, which accumulate between cells and fibres and act as the matrix (ground substance).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The matrix of connective tissues is formed by modified polysaccharides.

answer.text: Nucleic acids
Phospholipid bilayers
Modified polysaccharides
Chitinous plates

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q12 - Role of tendons and ligaments

questiontext.text: Tendons and ligaments are examples of dense regular connective tissue. What do they connect respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In dense regular connective tissues, collagen fibres are arranged in rows between many parallel bundles of fibres, providing high tensile strength along one axis.

Step 2: Functional Identification
Tendons attach skeletal muscles to bones, whereas ligaments attach one bone to another.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Tendons connect skeletal muscles to bones, and ligaments connect bone to bone.

answer.text: Bone to bone; skeletal muscle to bone
Epithelium to muscle; cartilage to bone
Smooth muscle to bone; skin to muscle
Skeletal muscle to bone; bone to bone

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q13 - Cells of areolar loose connective tissue

questiontext.text: Which combination of cells is found in areolar loose connective tissue beneath the skin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Loose connective tissue has cells and fibres loosely arranged in a semi-fluid ground substance.

Step 2: Identification of Cellular Components
Areolar tissue serves as a support framework for epithelium and contains fibroblasts (which produce and secrete fibres), macrophages, and mast cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Areolar tissue contains fibroblasts, macrophages, and mast cells.

answer.text: Fibroblasts, macrophages, and mast cells
Chondrocytes, osteocytes, and platelets
Goblet cells, neuroglia, and mast cells
Fibroblasts, osteocytes, and RBCs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q14 - Dense irregular connective tissue in skin

questiontext.text: Where is dense irregular connective tissue, characterised by fibroblasts and differently oriented collagen fibres, located?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dense connective tissues are divided into dense regular and dense irregular types based on the orientation of fibres.

Step 2: Structural and Location Analysis
Dense irregular connective tissue has fibroblasts and many fibres (mostly collagen) oriented in different directions, allowing it to resist stress from multiple angles. This tissue is present in the skin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Dense irregular connective tissue is present in the skin.

answer.text: In tendons and ligaments
In the skin
In the tip of the nose
In the bone marrow

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q15 - Locations of cartilage in adult humans

questiontext.text: In adults, cartilage with its solid, pliable, compression-resistant intercellular material is found in all of the following locations EXCEPT:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cartilage is a specialised connective tissue whose intercellular material is solid and pliable and resists compression, with chondrocytes enclosed in small cavities.

Step 2: Evaluation of Adult Locations
Most cartilages in vertebrate embryos are replaced by bones in adults. In adults, cartilage remains in the tip of the nose, outer ear joints, between adjacent bones of the vertebral column, and in limbs and hands. Long bones of the legs are composed of bone tissue, not cartilage.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cartilage does not form the weight-bearing shaft of long leg bones.

answer.text: Tip of the nose
Outer ear joints
Weight-bearing shaft of long leg bones
Between adjacent bones of the vertebral column

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q16 - Ground substance and functions of bone

questiontext.text: What gives bone its strength and hardness, and where are the bone cells (osteocytes) situated?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bone is a specialised connective tissue that provides the structural frame to the body, supports and protects softer organs, and houses bone marrow for blood cell production.

Step 2: Evaluation of Bone Matrix and Cells
Bones have a hard and non-pliable ground substance rich in calcium salts and collagen fibres, which give bone its strength. The bone cells, called osteocytes, are present in spaces called lacunae.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Calcium salts and collagen fibres give bone its strength, and osteocytes are situated in lacunae.

answer.text: Elastin fibres and modified polysaccharides; mast cells
Sodium salts and chitin; chondrocytes
Calcium salts and elastin fibres; plasma
Calcium salts and collagen fibres; lacunae

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q17 - Nutrient conversion in adipose tissue

questiontext.text: Excess nutrients that are not used immediately by the body are converted into fats and stored in which tissue, and how is it classified?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Connective tissues are divided into loose connective tissue, dense connective tissue, and specialised connective tissue.

Step 2: Evaluation of Adipose Tissue
Adipose tissue is a type of loose connective tissue located mainly beneath the skin. Its cells are specialised to store fats formed from excess nutrients that are not immediately used.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Excess nutrients are stored as fats in adipose tissue, which is classified as loose connective tissue.

answer.text: Adipose tissue; loose connective tissue
Areolar tissue; dense regular connective tissue
Adipose tissue; dense irregular connective tissue
Cartilage; specialised connective tissue

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q18 - Comparison of cartilage, bone, and blood

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly compares the three specialised connective tissues—cartilage, bone, and blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cartilage, bone, and blood are specialised connective tissues with distinct matrix properties and cellular components.

Step 2: Comparative Evaluation
Cartilage has a solid, pliable matrix that resists compression; bone has a hard, non-pliable ground substance rich in calcium salts and collagen fibres, with bone marrow producing blood cells; blood is a fluid connective tissue lacking secreted collagen or elastin fibres and containing plasma, RBCs, WBCs, and platelets.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cartilage has a solid pliable matrix, bone has a hard non-pliable matrix with blood cell production in bone marrow, and blood is a fluid matrix lacking secreted structural fibres.

answer.text: Cartilage has a non-pliable matrix; bone has a pliable matrix; blood cells secrete collagen fibres
Cartilage has a solid pliable matrix; bone has a hard non-pliable matrix with marrow producing blood cells; blood lacks secreted protein fibres
All three specialised connective tissues have fibroblasts that secrete elastin fibres
Bone cells are called chondrocytes, while cartilage cells are called osteocytes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q19 - Fine fibrils inside muscle fibres

questiontext.text: Each muscle is made of many long, cylindrical fibres arranged in parallel arrays. These muscle fibres are composed of numerous fine fibrils called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Muscle tissue is composed of elongated contractile cells called muscle fibres arranged in parallel arrays.

Step 2: Identification of Internal Fibrils
Each muscle fibre contains numerous fine contractile fibrils known as myofibrils, which enable contraction and relaxation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The fine fibrils inside muscle fibres are called myofibrils.

answer.text: Collagen fibrils
Neuroglia
Myofibrils
Ovarioles

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q20 - Characteristics of smooth muscle fibres

questiontext.text: Which of the following accurately describes smooth muscle fibres found in the walls of blood vessels, stomach, and intestine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Smooth muscles are one of the three muscle types (skeletal, smooth, cardiac) and line the walls of internal hollow organs.

Step 2: Structural and Functional Evaluation
Smooth muscle fibres taper at both ends (fusiform), do not show striations, are held together by cell junctions within a connective tissue sheath, and are involuntary in action.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Smooth muscle fibres are fusiform, non-striated, and involuntary.

answer.text: Cylindrical, striated, and voluntary
Branched, striated, and connected by intercalated discs
Fusiform, striated, and voluntary
Fusiform (tapering at both ends), non-striated, and involuntary

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q21 - Intercalated discs in cardiac muscle

questiontext.text: In cardiac muscle tissue, what is the specific function of intercalated discs located at fusion points of adjacent cell membranes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cardiac muscle tissue is a contractile tissue present exclusively in the heart, where cell junctions fuse plasma membranes of adjacent cells.

Step 2: Functional Analysis
Intercalated discs act as communication junctions at fusion points, allowing cardiac muscle cells to contract as a single unit—when one cell receives a signal to contract, its neighbours are also stimulated to contract.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Intercalated discs allow cardiac muscle cells to contract together as a coordinated unit.

answer.text: They act as communication junctions allowing cells to contract as a unit
They prevent substances from leaking across the heart wall
They attach cardiac muscle directly to skeletal bones
They store excess nutrients as fats between muscle bundles

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q22 - Volume and role of neuroglia

questiontext.text: What proportion of the volume of neural tissue in the human body is made up by neuroglial cells, and what is their primary role?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neural tissue consists of excitable neurons (the functional units of the neural system) and supporting neuroglial cells.

Step 2: Quantitative and Functional Evaluation
Neuroglial cells protect and support neurons and make up more than one-half the volume of neural tissue in our body.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Neuroglia make up more than one-half of neural tissue volume and serve to protect and support neurons.

answer.text: Less than one-tenth; generating electrical impulses
More than one-half; protecting and supporting neurons
Exactly one-quarter; contracting muscle fibres
More than three-quarters; secreting hormones into blood

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q23 - Signal propagation at neuron output zone

questiontext.text: When a neuron is suitably stimulated, an electrical disturbance travels along its plasma membrane. What happens upon its arrival at the neuron's endings (output zone)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neurons are excitable cells that exert the greatest control over the body's responsiveness to changing conditions.

Step 2: Mechanism at Output Zone
When an electrical disturbance reaches the neuron's endings or output zone, it triggers events that may cause either stimulation or inhibition of adjacent neurons and other cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Arrival of the electrical disturbance at the output zone may cause stimulation or inhibition of adjacent neurons and other cells.

answer.text: It always causes permanent inhibition of all neighbouring cells
It converts the neuron into a non-excitable neuroglial cell
It triggers events that may cause stimulation or inhibition of adjacent neurons and other cells
It is absorbed by collagen fibres of the connective tissue sheath

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q24 - Comparative sheath and junction features of muscles

questiontext.text: Which feature is shared by skeletal muscle bundles and smooth muscle bundles, as well as cardiac muscle cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All three muscle types (skeletal, smooth, and cardiac) are supported and organised by connective tissue, though their striations and voluntary control differ.

Step 2: Comparative Analysis
A sheath of tough connective tissue encloses bundles of skeletal muscle fibres, smooth muscle fibres are bundled together in a connective tissue sheath, and as noted in the chapter summary, connective tissue covers all three types of muscle tissues. In contrast, striations are absent in smooth muscles, and intercalated discs are unique to cardiac muscle.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All three types of muscle tissues are covered by connective tissue.

answer.text: Presence of prominent striations
Presence of intercalated discs
Direct voluntary control by conscious thought
Coverage by connective tissue

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q25 - Prostomium and peristomium in earthworm

questiontext.text: In an earthworm, what is the sensory lobe that serves as a covering for the mouth and acts as a wedge to force open cracks in the soil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The anterior end of an earthworm is specialised for burrowing through moist soil and ingesting organic matter.

Step 2: Identification of Anterior Structures
The first body segment containing the mouth is the peristomium (buccal segment), while the prostomium is an anterior lobe that covers the mouth, acts as a wedge to open soil cracks, and is sensory in function.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sensory wedge-like lobe covering the mouth is the prostomium.

answer.text: Prostomium
Peristomium
Clitellum
Typhlosole

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q26 - Segments lacking setae in earthworm

questiontext.text: In Pheretima, rows of S-shaped chitinous setae used for locomotion are present in every body segment EXCEPT:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Setae are S-shaped chitinous structures embedded in epidermal pits in the middle of each body segment that can be extended or retracted for locomotion.

Step 2: Evaluation of Distribution
Setae are present in every segment of the earthworm's body except the first segment (peristomium), the last segment, and the clitellum (segments 14–16).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Setae are absent in the first segment, last segment, and clitellum.

answer.text: Segments 1–5 and 10–11
The first segment, last segment, and clitellum
Only the clitellar segments 14–16
The preclitellar segments 1–13

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q27 - Function of calciferous glands in earthworm

questiontext.text: What is the specific role of calciferous glands present in the stomach (segments 9–14) of an earthworm?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Earthworms feed on decaying leaves and organic matter mixed with soil, which contains acidic humus.

Step 2: Physiological Role
Calciferous glands located in the stomach (segments 9–14) secrete substances that neutralise the humic acid present in humus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Calciferous glands neutralise the humic acid present in humus.

answer.text: Grinding soil particles and decaying leaves
Increasing the surface area of intestinal absorption
Neutralising the humic acid present in humus
Producing haemoglobin dissolved in blood plasma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q28 - Blood glands and haemoglobin in earthworm

questiontext.text: In Pheretima, blood glands are located on segments 4, 5, and 6. What do they produce, and where is the respiratory pigment located?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Earthworms exhibit a closed type of blood vascular system consisting of blood vessels, capillaries, and heart.

Step 2: Evaluation of Blood Glands
Blood glands in segments 4, 5, and 6 produce blood cells (which are phagocytic in nature) and haemoglobin. Unlike in vertebrates where haemoglobin is inside RBCs, in earthworms haemoglobin is dissolved in the blood plasma.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Blood glands produce phagocytic blood cells and haemoglobin dissolved in blood plasma.

answer.text: Nucleated RBCs containing intracellular haemoglobin
Haemolymph without respiratory pigment
Platelets and non-phagocytic leucocytes
Phagocytic blood cells and haemoglobin dissolved in blood plasma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q29 - Body wall layers of earthworm

questiontext.text: From outside to inside, what is the correct arrangement of layers in the body wall of an earthworm?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The body wall of the earthworm provides protection, secretion, and muscular movement for burrowing.

Step 2: Layer-by-Layer Order
Externally, the body wall is covered by a thin non-cellular cuticle. Below the cuticle lies the epidermis (a single layer of columnar epithelial cells containing secretory gland cells), followed by two muscle layers (outer circular and inner longitudinal), and an innermost coelomic epithelium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The outside-to-inside order is: Cuticle → Epidermis → Circular muscle → Longitudinal muscle → Coelomic epithelium.

answer.text: Cuticle → Epidermis → Circular muscle → Longitudinal muscle → Coelomic epithelium
Epidermis → Cuticle → Longitudinal muscle → Circular muscle → Coelomic epithelium
Cuticle → Coelomic epithelium → Circular muscle → Longitudinal muscle → Epidermis
Cuticle → Epidermis → Longitudinal muscle → Circular muscle → Coelomic epithelium

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q30 - Cocoon development in earthworm

questiontext.text: After mating in earthworms, where do fertilisation and embryonic development take place, and how many baby worms are typically produced per cocoon?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Earthworms exchange spermatophores during mating, and mature sperm, egg cells, and nutritive fluid are deposited into cocoons secreted by the gland cells of the clitellum.

Step 2: Quantitative and Developmental Details
Fertilisation and direct development (no larval stage) occur within the cocoons deposited in or on the soil. After about 3 weeks, each cocoon produces two to twenty baby worms, with an average of four.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fertilisation and development occur within cocoons, producing 2 to 20 baby worms with an average of four.

answer.text: Inside the spermathecae; 14–16 nymphs
Within cocoons; 2 to 20 baby worms (average of 4)
In freshwater; 2500–3000 tadpole larvae
Inside the ovarian funnel; exactly 1 baby worm

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q31 - Reproductive pore and gland segments in earthworm

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly states the segment positions of the female genital pore, male genital pores, testes, and accessory glands in Pheretima?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Earthworms are hermaphrodite, with male and female reproductive organs and openings arranged in specific anterior-midbody segments.

Step 2: Verification of Segment Numbers
A single median female genital pore is on the ventral side of the 14th segment. A pair of male genital pores is on the ventro-lateral sides of the 18th segment. Two pairs of testes are present in the 10th and 11th segments, and two pairs of accessory glands are located one pair each in the 17th and 19th segments.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Female genital pore is on segment 14, male genital pores on segment 18, testes in segments 10–11, and accessory glands in segments 17 and 19.

answer.text: Female pore: 18th; Male pores: 14th; Testes: 12th–13th; Accessory glands: 6th–9th
Female pore: 14th; Male pores: 18th; Testes: 6th–9th; Accessory glands: 10th–11th
Female pore: 14th; Male pores: 18th; Testes: 10th–11th; Accessory glands: 17th and 19th
Female pore: 12th; Male pores: 16th; Testes: 10th–11th; Accessory glands: 14th and 18th

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q32 - Anterior nerve ring and sensory system in earthworm

questiontext.text: How is the anterior nerve ring formed in the nervous system of an earthworm, and what sensory capabilities does the worm possess?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The nervous system of an earthworm is represented by ganglia arranged segmentwise on a ventral paired nerve cord.

Step 2: Anterior Nerve Ring and Sensory Receptors
In the 3rd and 4th segments, the ventral nerve cord bifurcates, laterally encircling the pharynx, and joins the cerebral ganglia dorsally to form a nerve ring. Earthworms lack eyes, but they possess light- and touch-sensitive receptor cells as well as specialised chemoreceptors (taste receptors) on the anterior part of the body.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The nerve cord bifurcates in segments 3–4 around the pharynx to join dorsal cerebral ganglia; earthworms lack eyes but have light, touch, and chemical receptors anteriorly.

answer.text: A dorsal nerve cord bifurcates in segments 10–11; compound eyes provide mosaic vision
The ventral nerve cord terminates at segment 14; tympanum detects ground vibrations
Cerebral ganglia lie ventrally in segment 18; simple eyes detect light intensity
The ventral nerve cord bifurcates in segments 3–4 around the pharynx to join dorsal cerebral ganglia; eyes are absent, but light, touch, and taste receptors are present anteriorly

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q33 - Exoskeleton sclerites and arthrodial membrane in cockroach

questiontext.text: In cockroaches, the hardened plates of the chitinous exoskeleton in each segment are called sclerites. What are the dorsal and ventral plates called, and what joins them?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The body of a cockroach is covered by a hard, brown chitinous exoskeleton segmented into hardened plates called sclerites.

Step 2: Identification of Plates and Membrane
Dorsally, the hardened plates are called tergites, and ventrally they are called sternites. Adjacent sclerites are joined by a thin and flexible articular membrane called the arthrodial membrane.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Dorsal plates are tergites, ventral plates are sternites, and they are joined by the arthrodial membrane.

answer.text: Tergites dorsally, sternites ventrally, joined by arthrodial membrane
Sternites dorsally, tergites ventrally, joined by pericardium
Phallomeres dorsally, ommatidia ventrally, joined by mesorchium
Cuticle dorsally, setae ventrally, joined by tympanum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q34 - Sexual dimorphism via anal styles and anal cerci

questiontext.text: Which external abdominal feature distinguishes a male cockroach from a female cockroach?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both male and female cockroaches have 10 abdominal segments, and both sexes bear a pair of jointed filamentous anal cerci on the 10th segment.

Step 2: Identification of Sex-Specific Feature
Male cockroaches bear a pair of short, thread-like anal styles that are absent in females.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The presence of a pair of short, thread-like anal styles distinguishes males from females.

answer.text: Presence of jointed filamentous anal cerci on the 10th segment
Presence of a pair of short, thread-like anal styles
Presence of 10 segments in the abdomen
Presence of a boat-shaped 7th sternum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q35 - Structure of gizzard in cockroach

questiontext.text: In the foregut of a cockroach, the gizzard (proventriculus) grinds food particles with the help of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The entire foregut of a cockroach is lined by cuticle and includes the pharynx, oesophagus, crop, and gizzard.

Step 2: Structural Evaluation of Gizzard
The gizzard has an outer layer of thick circular muscles and a thick inner cuticle forming six highly chitinous plates called teeth, which grind food particles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The gizzard grinds food using six highly chitinous plates called teeth formed by its inner cuticle.

answer.text: Calciferous glands that neutralise acids
Six to eight blind hepatic caecae
Six highly chitinous plates called teeth
One hundred to 150 Malpighian tubules

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q36 - Respiratory spiracles and tracheoles in cockroach

questiontext.text: How many pairs of spiracles open on the lateral side of a cockroach's body, and where does gaseous exchange actually occur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cockroaches respire through a network of tracheal tubes that deliver oxygen directly to body tissues.

Step 2: Quantitative and Physiological Evaluation
The tracheal system opens externally through 10 pairs of small holes called spiracles on the lateral sides, regulated by sphincters. Tracheal tubes subdivide into thin tracheoles, where exchange of gases takes place by diffusion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There are 10 pairs of spiracles, and gaseous exchange occurs at the tracheoles by diffusion.

answer.text: 4 pairs of spiracles; at the haemocoel by active transport
8 pairs of spiracles; at the ostia of the heart
12 pairs of spiracles; across the chitinous cuticle
10 pairs of spiracles; at the tracheoles by diffusion

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q37 - Distribution of ganglia in cockroach nervous system

questiontext.text: In the ventral nervous system of a cockroach, how many ganglia lie in the thorax and abdomen respectively, and why can a decapitated cockroach survive for up to a week?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The nervous system of a cockroach consists of fused, segmentally arranged ganglia joined by paired longitudinal connectives on the ventral side.

Step 2: Quantitative Distribution
Three ganglia lie in the thorax and six lie in the abdomen. Because the head holds only a small part of the nervous system (the supra-oesophageal ganglion) while the rest is distributed along the ventral part of the body, a cockroach can still live for as long as one week if its head is cut off.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There are 3 thoracic ganglia and 6 abdominal ganglia, and most of the nervous system is situated ventrally along the body.

answer.text: 3 in thorax and 6 in abdomen; most of the nervous system is situated along the ventral body
6 in thorax and 3 in abdomen; the heart generates nerve impulses
2 in thorax and 10 in abdomen; spiracles are controlled by the head alone
1 in thorax and 8 in abdomen; the crop stores neural signals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q38 - Compound eyes and mosaic vision in cockroach

questiontext.text: Each compound eye of a cockroach consists of about 2000 hexagonal ommatidia. What type of vision does this produce?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The compound eyes of cockroaches are situated on the dorsal surface of the head and are composed of numerous hexagonal units called ommatidia.

Step 2: Optical Characteristics
With the help of ~2000 ommatidia, a cockroach receives several images of an object, producing mosaic vision. This nocturnal vision is characterised by more sensitivity to light but less resolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
It produces mosaic vision with more sensitivity and less resolution.

answer.text: Simple vision with high resolution and low sensitivity
Mosaic vision with more sensitivity and less resolution
Binocular vision with high resolution and no sensitivity
Mosaic vision with less sensitivity and high resolution

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q39 - Accessory excretory structures in cockroach

questiontext.text: Besides Malpighian tubules, which three structures also assist in excretion in Periplaneta americana?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Excretion in cockroaches is primarily performed by Malpighian tubules, making the insect uricotelic.

Step 2: Identification of Accessory Excretory Structures
In addition to Malpighian tubules, the fat body, nephrocytes, and urecose glands also help in excretion in cockroaches.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fat body, nephrocytes, and urecose glands assist in excretion.

answer.text: Hepatic caecae, crop, and salivary glands
Phallomeres, collaterial glands, and spermatheca
Fat body, nephrocytes, and urecose glands
Septal nephridia, blood glands, and calciferous glands

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q40 - Ootheca production and nymphal moulting in cockroach

questiontext.text: On average, how many oothecae does a female Periplaneta americana produce, how many eggs are in each ootheca, and how many times does a nymph moult to become an adult?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cockroaches exhibit paurometabolous development through nymphal stages, with fertilised eggs encased in oothecae.

Step 2: Quantitative Evaluation
On average, a female cockroach produces 9–10 oothecae, each containing 14–16 eggs. The hatched nymph grows by moulting about 13 times to reach the adult form, with wing pads appearing in the next-to-last nymphal stage.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Females produce 9–10 oothecae with 14–16 eggs each, and nymphs moult about 13 times.

answer.text: 2–4 oothecae; 20–25 eggs each; 5 moults
14–16 oothecae; 9–10 eggs each; 8 moults
25–30 oothecae; 100 eggs each; 10 moults
9–10 oothecae; 14–16 eggs each; about 13 moults

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q41 - Skin and water absorption in frog

questiontext.text: How does the Indian bullfrog (Rana tigrina) obtain water, and why is its skin smooth and slippery?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Frogs are amphibians whose skin plays a vital role in water balance and cutaneous respiration.

Step 2: Physiological Evaluation
A frog never drinks water; instead, it absorbs water directly through its skin. The skin is always maintained in a moist, smooth, and slippery condition due to the presence of mucus secreted by mucous glands.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Frogs absorb water through the skin, which is kept smooth and slippery by mucus.

answer.text: It never drinks water but absorbs it through the skin; mucus keeps the skin smooth and slippery
It drinks water using its bilobed tongue; chitinous scales keep the skin slippery
It absorbs water only through the cloaca; fat bodies coat the skin
It drinks water through nostrils; sweat glands keep the skin moist

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q42 - Sexual dimorphism in frogs

questiontext.text: Which combination of external features distinguishes a male frog from a female frog?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Frogs exhibit clear external sexual dimorphism related to mating calls and amplexus.

Step 2: Identification of Male Features
Male frogs possess sound-producing vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimbs; both structures are absent in female frogs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Male frogs are distinguished by vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimbs.

answer.text: Presence of nictitating membrane and webbed hind feet
Presence of sound-producing vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimbs
Presence of five digits in forelimbs and four digits in hind limbs
Presence of a distinct neck and membranous tympanum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q43 - Bile and pancreatic juice action in frog duodenum

questiontext.text: In the digestive system of a frog, what are the respective roles of bile and pancreatic juice delivered to the duodenum through the common bile duct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Partially digested food (chyme) passes from the frog's stomach into the duodenum, where it receives bile from the gall bladder and pancreatic juice from the pancreas via a common bile duct.

Step 2: Functional Roles
Bile emulsifies fats, while pancreatic juice contains digestive enzymes that digest carbohydrates and proteins. Final digestion occurs in the intestine, followed by absorption through villi and microvilli.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Bile emulsifies fats, and pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins.

answer.text: Bile digests proteins; pancreatic juice neutralises humic acid
Bile digests carbohydrates; pancreatic juice emulsifies fats
Bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins
Both bile and pancreatic juice only absorb digested nutrients

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q44 - Blood cells and lymph composition in frog

questiontext.text: How do the red blood cells (RBCs) and lymph of a frog differ from mammalian RBCs and frog blood respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Frogs possess both a closed blood vascular system and a lymphatic system consisting of lymph, lymph channels, and lymph nodes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Blood and Lymph
Frog RBCs (erythrocytes) are nucleated and contain haemoglobin. Frog lymph differs from blood because it lacks a few proteins and RBCs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Frog RBCs are nucleated, and lymph lacks a few proteins and RBCs.

answer.text: Frog RBCs are enucleated; lymph contains more RBCs than blood
Frog RBCs lack haemoglobin; lymph contains platelets and RBCs
Frog RBCs are enucleated; lymph lacks WBCs completely
Frog RBCs are nucleated; lymph lacks a few proteins and RBCs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q45 - Portal systems in frog circulation

questiontext.text: Which two special venous connections are present in the circulatory system of a frog?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In frogs, veins collect blood from different parts of the body back to the heart, forming the venous system, which includes two specialised portal connections.

Step 2: Identification of Portal Systems
A special venous connection between the liver and intestine is called the hepatic portal system, and a special venous connection between the kidney and lower parts of the body is called the renal portal system.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Frogs possess both the hepatic portal system (liver–intestine) and the renal portal system (kidney–lower body).

answer.text: Hepatic portal system (between liver and intestine) and renal portal system (between kidney and lower parts of the body)
Pulmonary portal system (between lungs and heart) and cutaneous portal system (between skin and stomach)
Hepatic portal system (between kidney and liver) and cerebral portal system (between brain and heart)
Only a hepatic portal system; renal portal system is absent in frogs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q46 - Cranial nerves and brain divisions in frog

questiontext.text: How many pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain of a frog, and which structure is characteristic of the midbrain?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The frog's brain is enclosed in a bony cranium and divided into fore-brain, mid-brain, and hind-brain.

Step 2: Quantitative and Anatomical Evaluation
Ten pairs of cranial nerves arise from the frog's brain. Forebrain includes olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, and unpaired diencephalon; midbrain is characterised by a pair of optic lobes; hind-brain consists of cerebellum and medulla oblongata.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Frogs have 10 pairs of cranial nerves, and the midbrain is characterised by a pair of optic lobes.

answer.text: 12 pairs; cerebellum
10 pairs; a pair of optic lobes
10 pairs; olfactory lobes
8 pairs; unpaired diencephalon

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q47 - Sense organs and ear function in frog

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the organisation of sense organs in a frog?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Frogs possess five types of sense organs: touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (eyes), and hearing (tympanum with internal ears).

Step 2: Evaluation of Structural Complexity
Out of these, only the eyes and internal ears are well-organised structures, whereas touch, taste, and smell receptors are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. External ear is absent (only tympanum is seen externally), and the ear functions in both hearing and balancing (equilibrium).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Eyes (simple, one-unit) and internal ears (hearing and equilibrium) are well-organised structures, while touch, taste, and smell organs are cellular aggregations around nerve endings.

answer.text: All five sense organs are well-organised organs; eyes are compound with 2000 ommatidia
External ear pinnae are prominent; the internal ear performs hearing but not balancing
Eyes and internal ears are well-organised structures (the ear performs both hearing and equilibrium), whereas touch, taste, and smell organs are cellular aggregations around nerve endings
Taste buds and nasal epithelium are well-organised organs, whereas eyes are simple cellular aggregations

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STRUCTURALORGANISATIONINANIMALS_MCQ_Q48 - Excretion, ova count, and metamorphosis in frog

questiontext.text: Which combination of traits correctly characterises excretion and reproduction in Rana tigrina?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Frogs are amphibians with kidneys adapted for excreting urea and a reproductive cycle tied to freshwater.

Step 2: Verification of Excretory and Reproductive Traits
The frog excretes urea and is therefore a ureotelic animal. A mature female lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time, fertilisation is external in water, and development is indirect via a larval stage called tadpole, which undergoes metamorphosis to form the adult.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Frogs are ureotelic, lay 2500–3000 ova at a time, undergo external fertilisation in water, and develop indirectly through a tadpole larva.

answer.text: Uricotelic; 14–16 ova at a time; internal fertilisation; direct development
Ammonotelic; 2–20 ova at a time; external fertilisation; direct development
Ureotelic; 2500–3000 ova at a time; internal fertilisation; nymphal development
Ureotelic; 2500–3000 ova at a time; external fertilisation in water; indirect development via tadpole
